paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of history, the red fox was thought of as an animal of the countryside, a clever hunter of rabbits and an enemy of farmers who kept chickens. Today, however, many people are more likely to see a fox in a city street than in a field. Foxes are now found in towns and cities across Europe, North America and Australia, where they may be seen crossing roads at night, resting in gardens or even walking along railway platforms. Their success in such a different environment has made them a favourite subject for scientists who want to understand how wild animals adapt to life alongside humans.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In Britain, foxes seem to have moved into towns in large numbers during the 1930s. At that time, cities were spreading outwards as new suburbs were built, and many of these houses had long gardens with sheds, hedges and fruit trees. For a fox, such places offered everything it needed: food, shelter and quiet corners in which to raise young. Rather than the foxes arriving in the city, it might be more accurate to say that the city arrived around the foxes. Since then, foxes have been recorded in almost every large British city, although numbers vary greatly from one area to another.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One reason for the fox's success is that it is not a fussy eater. In the countryside, foxes eat small mammals, birds, insects and fruit. In cities, they eat many of the same things, but they also take advantage of food provided by people, whether on purpose or by accident. Studies of what urban foxes eat have shown that a large part of their diet comes from scraps, such as leftover meat and bread, as well as food deliberately put out by householders who enjoy watching them. Earthworms are another important source of food, especially on wet nights when they come to the surface of lawns and playing fields.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: City life has also changed fox behaviour in other ways. Urban foxes tend to have much smaller territories than rural ones, because food is easier to find in a limited area. A fox family in the countryside might need several square kilometres, while one in a city may live within a few streets. Researchers who have fitted foxes with tracking collars have found that the animals know their local area in great detail. They use the same routes night after night, moving along walls, through gaps in fences and under parked cars, and they generally avoid busy roads until the traffic has died down late at night.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Life in the city is not without danger, however. The biggest single cause of death for urban foxes is traffic, and young foxes are particularly at risk when they leave their parents in the autumn to look for a territory of their own. Disease is another threat. A skin condition called mange, which is caused by tiny mites, can spread quickly when foxes live close together, and it can make them lose most of their fur. As a result of these dangers, the average urban fox lives for only about two years, even though foxes kept in captivity can survive for more than ten.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is pleased to have foxes as neighbours. Common complaints include noise, particularly the loud screams that foxes make during the breeding season in winter, as well as the mess caused when they dig up gardens or tear open rubbish bags. Some people are also worried that foxes might attack pets or even children. In fact, attacks on people are extremely rare, and most cats are able to defend themselves against a fox, which is often similar in size. Experts say that the easiest way to reduce problems is to keep rubbish in bins with secure lids, rather than to try to remove the foxes themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Indeed, attempts to get rid of urban foxes have rarely been successful. When foxes are removed from an area, others quickly move in to take over the empty territory, so the number of animals soon returns to its previous level. For this reason, many local councils no longer offer to deal with foxes at all. Instead, they encourage residents to accept them as part of city wildlife. Some scientists also see urban foxes as a useful 'natural experiment', because watching how they change over the coming decades may help us to predict how other animals will cope as cities continue to grow.

title: The Simple Box That Changed World Trade
titleCn: 改变世界贸易的铁箱子：集装箱

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost everything we buy, from clothes and phones to bananas and furniture, has spent part of its journey inside a large metal box. The shipping container is so common today that most people hardly notice the stacks of red, blue and grey boxes in ports or on the backs of lorries. Yet the container was only introduced in the middle of the twentieth century, and it has been described as one of the most important inventions of modern times. It did not depend on any new science. Its power came from a simple idea: that goods should be packed once and then moved all the way to their destination without being unpacked.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Before containers, loading a ship was slow, hard and expensive work. Goods arrived at the port in sacks, barrels, crates and bundles of every shape and size. Teams of dock workers carried them on board one by one and fitted them into the ship's hold, a process that could take a week or more for a single vessel. Ships often spent almost as much time in port as they did at sea. Theft was also a serious problem, because goods passed through so many hands. As a result, loading and unloading made up a large part of the total cost of sending goods by sea.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The person usually given credit for the container is Malcom McLean, an American who owned a trucking company. According to a popular story, he had the idea in 1937 while waiting for hours at a port for his lorry to be unloaded. Whether or not the story is true, it was not until 1956 that he put his idea into practice. In that year, a converted oil tanker called the Ideal X sailed from New Jersey to Texas carrying fifty-eight containers on its deck. McLean calculated that the cost of loading the ship was a small fraction of the usual price, a result that persuaded him to invest heavily in the new system.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: At first, however, the new system faced serious obstacles. Different companies built containers of different sizes, so a box from one shipping line might not fit on the ships, cranes or lorries of another. Dock workers' unions, fearing that the change would destroy thousands of jobs, opposed it strongly in many ports. The first problem was solved in the late 1960s, when international agreements set standard sizes. The most widely used containers today are twenty or forty feet long, and port traffic is still measured in 'twenty-foot equivalent units', or TEUs. The second problem proved harder, and in many places the unions' fears turned out to be justified.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The container changed the shape of ports as well as the work done in them. Huge cranes, large flat storage areas and good road and rail links became essential, and these could rarely be found in the old harbours in the centre of cities. New container terminals were therefore built further away, often near the mouth of a river where deeper water allowed larger ships to enter. In cities such as London and New York, the old docks fell silent, and the warehouses beside them were later turned into offices, flats and museums.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The effects on world trade were enormous. Because containers made transport cheaper and more reliable, it became practical for companies to produce goods in one country, assemble them in another and sell them in a third. Factories no longer needed to be close to their customers. Some economists argue that the container did more to increase international trade than all the trade agreements signed in the same period. Today, the largest ships can carry more than twenty thousand standard containers, and a box can travel from Asia to Europe in around a month.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The container has its critics, too. Because so many boxes travel on each ship, customs officers are able to inspect only a small proportion of them, which makes smuggling a concern. Containers are also lost at sea during storms every year, and their contents can wash up on beaches far away. Meanwhile, empty containers are a common sight in some ports, because trade between regions is often unbalanced and the boxes have to be sent back without any goods inside. Engineers are now experimenting with folding containers that would take up less space when empty, although these have yet to be widely adopted.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few feelings have such a bad reputation as boredom. We complain about boring meetings, boring journeys and boring jobs, and parents often feel they have failed if their children say they have nothing to do. Many of us now carry a phone that can fill every spare moment with news, games or messages, so that we hardly ever have to experience boredom at all. Yet a growing number of psychologists believe that this may be a mistake. In my view, boredom is not simply an unpleasant state to be avoided at any cost. Used in the right way, it may be one of the most useful feelings we have.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Researchers define boredom as the uncomfortable feeling of wanting to be busy with something satisfying but being unable to find it. It is different from relaxation, which is a pleasant state of rest, and from apathy, in which a person does not care about doing anything at all. A bored person does care: they want something to happen, and their mind is searching for it. This restless searching is the key to understanding why boredom exists. Like hunger, which pushes us to look for food, boredom seems to push us to look for something more rewarding to do with our time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some evidence for the positive side of boredom comes from an experiment carried out in Britain. One group of volunteers was asked to copy numbers from a telephone directory for fifteen minutes, a task that almost everyone finds dull. A second group went straight on to the next stage. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The volunteers who had first done the boring task came up with more ideas, and their ideas were judged to be more original. The researchers suggested that boredom had encouraged their minds to wander, and that this daydreaming had helped them think creatively.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficulty today is that boredom rarely lasts long enough to have this effect. As soon as we feel the first sign of it, while waiting for a bus or standing in a queue, we reach for our phones. Studies suggest that many people check their phones dozens of times a day, often without any clear reason. I believe that this habit has a cost that is rarely discussed. By escaping from boredom so quickly, we deny our minds the empty time they need to make unexpected connections between ideas, to plan for the future or simply to reflect on our own lives.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Children may lose the most. Many families now fill their children's free time with organised activities, from music lessons to sports clubs, partly because parents fear that a bored child is an unhappy one. These activities certainly have value. However, some educational experts argue that children also need unstructured time in which nobody tells them what to do. It is often in these moments that they invent games, build things or discover an interest that lasts for life. In my opinion, a child who complains of having nothing to do should not always be rescued immediately.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This does not mean that all boredom is good. Long periods of boredom, especially at work or school, have been linked to poor concentration, mistakes and low mood. People who feel bored most of the time are more likely to eat unhealthy snacks or to take risks simply to feel something. The problem in these cases is not a short period of boredom but the sense of being trapped in a situation that has no meaning. It would therefore be wrong to suggest that employers should make jobs more boring in the hope of producing creative workers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should we do? The answer is not to seek out boredom deliberately, but to stop running away from it. Leaving the phone in a pocket during a short train journey, or going for a walk without headphones, gives the mind a chance to wander. Many writers and scientists have described how their best ideas came to them while they were doing something quite dull, such as having a shower or waiting for a kettle to boil. Boredom, it seems, is less an enemy than a messenger, telling us that it is time to find something more meaningful to do.

evidence.quote: boredom had encouraged their minds to wander

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: In paragraph B, the writer compares boredom to hunger in order to show that boredom

options.text: is a physical rather than a mental feeling.
pushes people to look for something better to do.
is more common when people are tired.
disappears if it is ignored for long enough.

questions.explanation: B 段末：就像饥饿推动我们去找食物，无聊推动我们去找更有意义的事做。对应 B。A、C、D 原文都没提。

evidence.quote: Like hunger, which pushes us to look for food, boredom seems to push us to look for something more rewarding to do with our time.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph F, long periods of boredom

options.text: make people more creative.
are connected with poor concentration and low mood.
are less harmful at work than at school.
usually lead to healthier habits.

questions.explanation: F 段：长期无聊与注意力差、出错和情绪低落有关（have been linked to）。对应 B。A 是短时无聊的好处，不是长期的；C 原文没有比较；D 与原文相反（更可能吃不健康的零食）。

evidence.quote: Long periods of boredom, especially at work or school, have been linked to poor concentration, mistakes and low mood.

questions.prompt: What does the writer think about making jobs more boring?

options.text: It would make workers more creative.
It is a mistaken idea.
Some employers have already tried it.
It only works for short periods.

questions.explanation: F 段末：作者说，因此认为雇主应该让工作更无聊、好让员工更有创造力，是错误的（It would therefore be wrong）。对应 B。A 正是作者否定的观点；C、D 原文没提。

evidence.quote: It would therefore be wrong to suggest that employers should make jobs more boring in the hope of producing creative workers.

questions.prompt: What does the writer recommend in the final paragraph?

options.text: choosing boring activities on purpose
not escaping from boredom so quickly
listening to music while walking
taking more showers to get new ideas

questions.explanation: G 段：办法不是刻意去找无聊（排除 A），而是不再逃避它（stop running away from it）。对应 B。C 与原文相反（原文建议不戴耳机散步）；D 是把例子当成了建议。

evidence.quote: The answer is not to seek out boredom deliberately, but to stop running away from it.
